text:
A reaction is carried out in aqueous solution in a polystyrene cup. The temperature of the solution decreases during the reaction.

Which statement is correct?

A. Heat is transferred from the system to the surroundings and $\Delta H$ is negative.
B. Heat is transferred from the surroundings to the system and $\Delta H$ is positive.
C. Heat is transferred from the surroundings to the system and $\Delta H$ is negative.
D. Heat is transferred from the system to the surroundings and $\Delta H$ is positive.
ms: **B.** A temperature fall in the solution (the surroundings) means energy is absorbed by the reacting system: the reaction is endothermic, so $\Delta H$ is positive. A describes an exothermic reaction; C and D combine a direction of heat flow with the wrong sign of $\Delta H$.

text:
The potential energy profile for a reaction is shown.

![Potential energy profile with arrows P, Q and R](qbank/img/gen_chem_R1.1_2.svg)

Which row correctly identifies the activation energy of the forward reaction and the enthalpy change, $\Delta H$, of the forward reaction?

A. activation energy: P; $\Delta H$: R, positive
B. activation energy: Q; $\Delta H$: R, positive
C. activation energy: P; $\Delta H$: R, negative
D. activation energy: Q; $\Delta H$: P, negative
ms: **A.** The forward activation energy is measured from the reactants up to the transition state (P). R is the difference between products and reactants; the products are higher in energy, so the reaction is endothermic and $\Delta H$ is positive. Q is the activation energy of the reverse reaction (B, D); C gives the wrong sign.

text:
When $0.0100\ \text{mol}$ of a solid dissolves in $50.0\ \text{g}$ of water, the temperature of the water rises by $4.0\ \text{K}$. The specific heat capacity of water is $4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.

Which expression gives the enthalpy change of solution, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$?

A. $-\dfrac{50.0 \times 4.18 \times 4.0}{0.0100}$
B. $-\dfrac{50.0 \times 4.18 \times 4.0}{1000 \times 0.0100}$
C. $+\dfrac{50.0 \times 4.18 \times 4.0}{1000 \times 0.0100}$
D. $-\dfrac{50.0 \times 4.18 \times (4.0 + 273)}{1000 \times 0.0100}$
ms: **B.** $q = mc\Delta T$ gives joules, so divide by 1000 for kJ and by the amount in mol; the temperature rises, so the process is exothermic and $\Delta H$ is negative. A gives J mol$^{-1}$, C has the wrong sign, and D wrongly converts the temperature *change* to kelvin by adding 273 (a change of 4.0 °C is already a change of 4.0 K).

text:
Which conditions are used to define standard enthalpy changes, $\Delta H^{\ominus}$?

A. 273 K, 100 kPa, concentration of solutions $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$
B. 298 K, 100 kPa, concentration of solutions $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$
C. 298 K, 100 kPa, all reactants and products in the gaseous state
D. 273 K, 101 kPa, concentration of solutions $1\ \text{g dm}^{-3}$
ms: **B.** Standard conditions are a pressure of 100 kPa and solutions of concentration $1\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$, with substances in their standard states; enthalpy data are normally quoted at 298 K. A and D use 273 K (STP for gases), D uses mass concentration, and C wrongly requires all substances to be gases (substances are in their standard states, e.g. $\ce{H2O(l)}$).

text:
A student determines the enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol by using a spirit burner to heat water in a glass beaker. The experimental value is much less exothermic than the data booklet value.

Which change to the method would most improve the **accuracy** of the result?

A. Using a thermometer with a finer scale
B. Burning the fuel for a longer time
C. Replacing the beaker with a copper can fitted with a lid and surrounded by a draught shield
D. Repeating the experiment three times and calculating a mean
ms: **C.** The large discrepancy is a systematic error caused mainly by heat loss to the surroundings; a copper can (good conductor, low heat capacity) with a lid and draught shield reduces this loss. A and D only reduce random error (improve precision), and burning for longer (B) does not reduce the proportion of heat lost.

text:
A student determined the enthalpy change of neutralization of hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide solution.

- $25.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of $1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\ce{HCl(aq)}$ was placed in a polystyrene cup and its temperature recorded every minute.
- At 3.0 min, $25.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of $1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\ce{NaOH(aq)}$, at the same initial temperature, was added and the mixture stirred.
- The temperature was then recorded every minute from 4.0 min to 12.0 min.

![Temperature against time: 21.0 °C for 0 to 2 min, then falling steadily from 27.4 °C at 4 min to 25.8 °C at 12 min](qbank/img/gen_chem_R1.1_6.svg)

$$\ce{HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)}$$

(a) Explain why the maximum temperature is found by extrapolating the cooling line back to 3.0 min, rather than by using the highest temperature recorded. [2]

(b) Determine the temperature change, $\Delta T$, from the graph. [1]

(c) Calculate the enthalpy change of neutralization, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Assume the solution has a density of $1.00\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$ and a specific heat capacity of $4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$. [3]

(d) The literature value is $-57.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Calculate the percentage error in the student's value. [1]

(e) Predict, with a reason, the temperature change if the experiment were repeated using $50.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of each solution. [2]

(f) Suggest why a polystyrene cup is used rather than a glass beaker. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- heat is lost to the surroundings while the reaction/mixing takes place / the temperature is already falling by the time the first reading is taken ✓
- extrapolation gives the temperature that would have been reached if the reaction were instantaneous with no heat loss / compensates for heat loss ✓

**(b)**
- $\Delta T = 27.6 - 21.0 = 6.6\ \text{K}$ ✓ Accept 6.5 – 6.7 K.

**(c)**
- $q = 50.0 \times 4.18 \times 6.6 = 1380\ \text{J}$ / $1.38\ \text{kJ}$ ✓
- $n(\ce{H2O}) = 0.0250 \times 1.00 = 0.0250\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $\Delta H = -\dfrac{1.38}{0.0250} = -55.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Negative sign required for M3. Award [3] for correct final answer. ECF from (b) (range −54.3 to −56.0).

**(d)**
- $\dfrac{57.2 - 55.2}{57.2} \times 100 = 3.5\%$ ✓ ECF from (c).

**(e)**
- $\Delta T$ is the same / 6.6 K ✓
- amount reacting (and heat released) doubles but the mass of solution heated also doubles ✓

Do not accept "doubles" for M1.

**(f)**
- polystyrene is a (thermal) insulator / has low heat capacity so less heat is lost or absorbed by the cup ✓

text:
Ammonium nitrate dissolves in water:

$$\ce{NH4NO3(s) -> NH4+(aq) + NO3-(aq)}$$

A student added $5.00\ \text{g}$ of ammonium nitrate to $50.0\ \text{g}$ of water in a polystyrene cup. The temperature fell from 22.5 °C to 15.3 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is $4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.

(a) State, with a reason, whether the dissolving process is exothermic or endothermic. [1]

(b) Calculate the heat energy, in J, absorbed from the water. [1]

(c) Calculate the enthalpy change of solution of ammonium nitrate, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. [2]

(d) During the experiment some heat is transferred from the room into the cup. Explain the effect this has on the calculated enthalpy change compared with the true value. [2]

(e) Sketch an enthalpy level diagram for the dissolving process, labelling $\Delta H$. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- endothermic **and** the temperature of the water/surroundings decreases (heat is absorbed from the water) ✓

**(b)**
- $q = 50.0 \times 4.18 \times 7.2 = 1.50 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J}$ (1504.8 J) ✓

**(c)**
- $n(\ce{NH4NO3}) = \dfrac{5.00}{80.06} = 0.0625\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $\Delta H = +\dfrac{1.50}{0.0625} = +24.1\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Positive sign required for M2. Award [2] for correct final answer. ECF from (b). Accept 24.0 – 24.1.

**(d)**
- heat gained from the room means the temperature falls by less / measured $\Delta T$ is smaller than the true value ✓
- calculated $\Delta H$ is less positive / smaller in magnitude than the true value ✓

**(e)**

![Enthalpy level diagram: products higher than reactants, upward arrow labelled ΔH = +24.1 kJ/mol](qbank/img/gen_chem_R1.1_7.svg)

- products ($\ce{NH4+(aq) + NO3-(aq)}$) shown at a higher enthalpy level than reactants ($\ce{NH4NO3(s)}$ + water) ✓
- arrow from reactants to products labelled $\Delta H$ (positive / +24.1 kJ mol$^{-1}$) **and** vertical axis labelled enthalpy ✓

text:
A student used a spirit burner to heat water in a copper can and determine the enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol, $\ce{C2H5OH}$ ($M = 46.08\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$). The results are shown.

| Measurement | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass of burner and ethanol before burning / g ($\pm 0.01$) | 152.46 |
| Mass of burner and ethanol after burning / g ($\pm 0.01$) | 151.88 |
| Mass of water / g | 150.0 |
| Initial temperature of water / °C ($\pm 0.5$) | 18.5 |
| Final temperature of water / °C ($\pm 0.5$) | 31.0 |

Specific heat capacity of water $= 4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.

(a) Write an equation for the complete combustion of ethanol. [1]

(b) Calculate the amount, in mol, of ethanol burned. [1]

(c) Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. [2]

(d) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in your answer to (c), using the uncertainties shown in the table. Ignore the uncertainty in the mass of water. [3]

(e) The literature value is $-1367\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Deduce, with reference to your answer to (d), whether random errors alone can account for the difference between the experimental and literature values. [2]

(f) Suggest **two** modifications to the method that would reduce the systematic error. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- $\ce{C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) -> 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l)}$ ✓ State symbols not required.

**(b)**
- mass burned $= 0.58\ \text{g}$; $n = \dfrac{0.58}{46.08} = 0.0126\ \text{mol}$ ✓

**(c)**
- $q = 150.0 \times 4.18 \times 12.5 = 7840\ \text{J}$ / $7.84\ \text{kJ}$ ✓
- $\Delta H_c = -\dfrac{7.84}{0.0126} = -623\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Accept −620 to −625 depending on rounding. Negative sign required. ECF from (b).

**(d)**
- mass: $\dfrac{0.02}{0.58} \times 100 = 3.4\%$ ✓
- temperature change: $\dfrac{1.0}{12.5} \times 100 = 8.0\%$ ✓
- total $= 3.4 + 8.0 = 11\%$ (11.4%) ✓

Award [2 max] if ±0.01 g and ±0.5 °C are used (single reading uncertainties) giving 1.7% + 4.0% = 5.7%.

**(e)**
- uncertainty range is about ±70 kJ mol$^{-1}$ / experimental value lies between about −550 and −695 kJ mol$^{-1}$ ✓
- literature value lies far outside this range / the difference (about 54%) is much greater than 11%, so random errors cannot account for it; systematic errors (e.g. heat loss, incomplete combustion) must be present ✓

ECF from (c) and (d).

**(f)** Any two, ✓ each:
- insulate the can / use a lid / use a draught shield
- reduce the distance between the flame and the can
- use a calorimeter with an oxygen supply (bomb calorimeter) to ensure complete combustion
- put the cap on the burner as soon as heating stops / weigh immediately to reduce evaporation of ethanol
- determine the heat capacity of the apparatus (calibrate) and include it in the calculation

Do not accept "repeat the experiment" or "use more precise instruments".

text:
Excess zinc powder was added to $50.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of $0.200\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ copper(II) sulfate solution in a polystyrene cup. After correcting for heat loss, the temperature rise was $10.3\ \text{K}$.

Assume the solution has a density of $1.00\ \text{g cm}^{-3}$ and a specific heat capacity of $4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$, and that the heat capacity of the cup and the zinc can be ignored.

(a) Write the ionic equation, including state symbols, for the reaction. [1]

(b) Calculate the enthalpy change, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, for the reaction as written in (a). [3]

(c) Another student repeated the experiment using $0.500\ \text{g}$ of zinc powder with the same volume and concentration of copper(II) sulfate solution. Deduce, showing your working, the expected temperature rise. [3]

(d) Predict the temperature rise if $100.0\ \text{cm}^3$ of the same copper(II) sulfate solution were used with excess zinc. [1]

(e) Suggest why zinc powder is used rather than large pieces of zinc. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- $\ce{Zn(s) + Cu^{2+}(aq) -> Zn^{2+}(aq) + Cu(s)}$ ✓ State symbols required.

**(b)**
- $q = 50.0 \times 4.18 \times 10.3 = 2150\ \text{J}$ (2152.7 J) ✓
- $n(\ce{Cu^{2+}}) = 0.0500 \times 0.200 = 0.0100\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $\Delta H = -\dfrac{2.15}{0.0100} = -215\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Negative sign required for M3. Award [3] for correct final answer.

**(c)**
- $n(\ce{Zn}) = \dfrac{0.500}{65.38} = 7.65 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- this is less than $0.0100\ \text{mol}$ $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ so zinc is now the limiting reactant ✓
- $\Delta T = 10.3 \times \dfrac{7.65 \times 10^{-3}}{0.0100} = 7.9\ \text{K}$ ✓

Accept alternative method: $q = 7.65 \times 10^{-3} \times 215\,000 = 1640\ \text{J}$, $\Delta T = 1640 / (50.0 \times 4.18) = 7.9\ \text{K}$. ECF from (b). Award [1 max] for 10.3 K with no recognition that zinc is limiting.

**(d)**
- 10.3 K (amount reacting and mass of solution both double) ✓

**(e)**
- larger surface area so the reaction is faster/complete in a shorter time, so less heat is lost during the reaction ✓

text:
Which statement is correct for an exothermic reaction?

A. More energy is absorbed in breaking bonds than is released in forming bonds.
B. More energy is released in forming bonds than is absorbed in breaking bonds.
C. Bond breaking releases energy and bond forming absorbs energy.
D. The products have a greater enthalpy than the reactants.
ms: **B.** Bond breaking is endothermic and bond forming is exothermic; when more energy is released by the new bonds than is absorbed in breaking the old ones, $\Delta H$ is negative. A describes an endothermic reaction, C reverses the energy changes, and D describes an endothermic reaction.

text:
Use the bond enthalpies given to calculate the enthalpy change, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, for the reaction:

$$\ce{H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2HCl(g)}$$

| Bond | Bond enthalpy / $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |
|---|---|
| H–H | 436 |
| Cl–Cl | 242 |
| H–Cl | 431 |

A. $-247$
B. $-184$
C. $+184$
D. $+247$
ms: **B.** $\Delta H = \sum(\text{bonds broken}) - \sum(\text{bonds formed}) = (436 + 242) - 2(431) = -184\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. C reverses the subtraction; D counts only one H–Cl bond formed ($678 - 431 = +247$), and A combines this error with the reversed subtraction.

text:
The enthalpy level diagram shows the formation of carbon dioxide from carbon by two routes.

![Enthalpy level diagram: C(s)+O2(g) to CO2(g) −394; C(s)+O2(g) to CO(g)+½O2(g) ΔHx; CO(g)+½O2(g) to CO2(g) −283](qbank/img/gen_chem_R1.2_3.svg)

What is the value of $\Delta H_x$, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$?

A. $-677$
B. $-111$
C. $+111$
D. $+677$
ms: **B.** By Hess's law, $-394 = \Delta H_x + (-283)$, so $\Delta H_x = -394 + 283 = -111\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. C has the wrong sign (CO is below C + O$_2$ on the diagram); A and D add the two values instead of subtracting.

text:
Which process is exothermic?

A. $\ce{Na(s) -> Na(g)}$
B. $\ce{Na(g) -> Na+(g) + e-}$
C. $\ce{Cl(g) + e- -> Cl-(g)}$
D. $\ce{O-(g) + e- -> O^{2-}(g)}$
ms: **C.** The first electron affinity of chlorine is exothermic ($-349\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) because the added electron is attracted by the nucleus. Atomization (A) and ionization (B) require energy, and the second electron affinity of oxygen (D) is endothermic because the electron is added to an already negative ion, which repels it.

text:
Which compound has the largest lattice enthalpy?

A. NaCl
B. KCl
C. CaO
D. MgO
ms: **D.** Lattice enthalpy increases with greater ionic charge and smaller ionic radius. MgO and CaO have 2+ and 2− ions (much stronger attraction than the 1+/1− ions in NaCl and KCl), and $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ is smaller than $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$, so MgO has the largest value.

text:
The standard enthalpies of formation of some substances are given.

| Substance | $\Delta H_f^{\ominus}$ / $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |
|---|---|
| $\ce{CH4(g)}$ | $-75$ |
| $\ce{CO2(g)}$ | $-394$ |
| $\ce{H2O(l)}$ | $-286$ |

What is the standard enthalpy change, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, for the reaction below?

$$\ce{CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)}$$

A. $+891$
B. $-605$
C. $-891$
D. $-1041$
ms: **C.** $\Delta H^{\ominus} = \sum \Delta H_f^{\ominus}(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^{\ominus}(\text{reactants}) = [-394 + 2(-286)] - (-75) = -891\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ($\Delta H_f^{\ominus}$ of $\ce{O2}$ is zero). B ignores the coefficient 2 for water, D adds instead of subtracts the methane value, and A reverses the subtraction.

text:
The enthalpy change of hydration of anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, $\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}$, cannot be measured directly. It was determined using the energy cycle shown.

$$\ce{CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l) -> CuSO4.5H2O(s)}$$

![Energy cycle: CuSO4(s)+5H2O(l) to CuSO4·5H2O(s) by ΔH(hyd); both dissolve in excess water to CuSO4(aq) by ΔH1 and ΔH2](qbank/img/gen_chem_R1.2_7.svg)

- **Experiment 1:** $4.00\ \text{g}$ of anhydrous $\ce{CuSO4}$ ($M = 159.62\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) was added to $50.0\ \text{g}$ of water. The temperature **rose** by $7.5\ \text{K}$.
- **Experiment 2:** $6.25\ \text{g}$ of $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ ($M = 249.72\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) was added to $50.0\ \text{g}$ of water. The temperature **fell** by $1.3\ \text{K}$.

Assume that only the $50.0\ \text{g}$ of water is heated or cooled and that its specific heat capacity is $4.18\ \text{J g}^{-1}\ \text{K}^{-1}$.

(a) Suggest why $\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}$ cannot be measured directly. [1]

(b) Calculate $\Delta H_1$, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. [2]

(c) Calculate $\Delta H_2$, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. [2]

(d) Determine $\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}$, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, using the energy cycle. [2]

(e) The literature value of $\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}$ is $-78.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Suggest why heat exchange with the surroundings affects experiment 1 more than experiment 2, and state the effect this has on the value of $\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}$ obtained. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- it is not possible to add exactly 5 mol of water per mole of solid so that only the hydrate forms (excess water dissolves the solid) / the reaction of a solid with water is slow and the temperature change of a solid cannot easily be measured ✓

**(b)**
- $q = 50.0 \times 4.18 \times 7.5 = 1568\ \text{J}$ **and** $n = \dfrac{4.00}{159.62} = 0.02506\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $\Delta H_1 = -\dfrac{1.568}{0.02506} = -62.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Negative sign required.

**(c)**
- $q = 50.0 \times 4.18 \times 1.3 = 272\ \text{J}$ **and** $n = \dfrac{6.25}{249.72} = 0.02503\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $\Delta H_2 = +\dfrac{0.272}{0.02503} = +10.9\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Positive sign required.

**(d)**
- $\Delta H_{\text{hyd}} = \Delta H_1 - \Delta H_2$ ✓
- $= -62.6 - 10.9 = -73.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Accept −73.4 to −73.5. ECF from (b) and (c).

**(e)**
- experiment 1 has a much larger temperature change, so the solution is further from room temperature and the rate of heat loss is greater ✓
- $\Delta H_1$ is less negative than the true value so $\Delta H_{\text{hyd}}$ is less negative/less exothermic than the true value ✓

text:
Hydrazine, $\ce{N2H4}$, has been used as a rocket fuel. It reacts with oxygen as follows:

$$\ce{N2H4(g) + O2(g) -> N2(g) + 2H2O(g)}$$

| Bond | Bond enthalpy / $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |
|---|---|
| N–N | 158 |
| N–H | 391 |
| O=O | 498 |
| N≡N | 945 |
| O–H | 463 |

(a) Draw the Lewis (electron dot) formula of hydrazine. [1]

(b) Calculate the enthalpy change for the reaction using the bond enthalpies given. [3]

(c) The value calculated using standard enthalpies of formation is $-579\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Suggest why the value in (b) differs from this. [1]

(d) Predict, with a reason, whether the enthalpy change would be more or less exothermic if the water were produced as a liquid. [2]

(e) Suggest one advantage, other than the energy released, of using hydrazine as a rocket fuel. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- two N atoms joined by a single bond, each N also bonded to two H atoms, **and** one lone pair on each N ✓

Accept dots, crosses or lines for bonding pairs.

**(b)**
- bonds broken: $158 + 4(391) + 498 = 2220\ \text{kJ}$ ✓
- bonds formed: $945 + 4(463) = 2797\ \text{kJ}$ ✓
- $\Delta H = 2220 - 2797 = -577\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Award [3] for correct final answer. Award [2 max] for +577.

**(c)**
- bond enthalpies are average values (from a range of compounds) and not specific to these molecules ✓

**(d)**
- more exothermic ✓
- condensation of water (forming intermolecular forces/hydrogen bonds) releases energy / liquid water has lower enthalpy than gaseous water ✓

**(e)**
- products are gases (large volume of gas produced, giving thrust) / products ($\ce{N2}$ and $\ce{H2O}$) are non-polluting / no $\ce{CO2}$ is produced ✓

text:
The Born–Haber cycle for magnesium chloride is shown. All values are in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

![Born–Haber cycle for MgCl2: +148, +242, +738, +1451, −698, ΔHf −641 and lattice enthalpy X](qbank/img/gen_chem_R1.2_9.svg)

(a) Write equations, with state symbols, for the processes that have enthalpy changes of $+1451\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $-698\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. [2]

(b) Determine the value of X, the lattice enthalpy of magnesium chloride. [2]

(c) The lattice enthalpy of magnesium chloride calculated using a purely ionic model is $2326\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Explain why the value from the Born–Haber cycle is larger. [2]

(d) Predict, with a reason, whether the lattice enthalpy of magnesium oxide is larger or smaller than that of magnesium chloride. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- $\ce{Mg+(g) -> Mg^{2+}(g) + e-}$ ✓
- $\ce{2Cl(g) + 2e- -> 2Cl-(g)}$ ✓

Accept $\ce{Cl(g) + e- -> Cl-(g)}$ with a statement that the value is for 2 mol. State symbols required.

**(b)**
- $X = 641 + 148 + 242 + 738 + 1451 - 698$ ✓
- $X = +2522\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Award [2] for correct final answer. Award [1 max] for −2522 or for an answer that uses +641.

**(c)**
- the bonding in $\ce{MgCl2}$ has some covalent character ✓
- the small, highly charged $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ ion polarizes/distorts the electron cloud of the large $\ce{Cl-}$ ion, giving additional attraction ✓

**(d)**
- larger ✓
- $\ce{O^{2-}}$ has a greater charge (and smaller radius) than $\ce{Cl-}$, so the electrostatic attraction between the ions is stronger ✓

text:
Standard enthalpy changes of combustion are given.

| Substance | $\Delta H_c^{\ominus}$ / $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ |
|---|---|
| $\ce{C}$(s, graphite) | $-394$ |
| $\ce{H2(g)}$ | $-286$ |
| $\ce{C2H5OH(l)}$ | $-1367$ |

(a) Write an equation, with state symbols, for the reaction that represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol. [1]

(b) Suggest why the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol cannot be measured directly. [1]

(c) Determine the standard enthalpy change of formation of ethanol using an energy cycle and the data given. [3]

(d) The standard enthalpy change of formation of gaseous ethanol is $-235\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Use your answer to (c) to calculate the enthalpy change of vaporization of ethanol, and explain why it is positive. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- $\ce{2C(s) + 3H2(g) + 1/2O2(g) -> C2H5OH(l)}$ ✓ State symbols required.

**(b)**
- carbon, hydrogen and oxygen do not react directly to form (only) ethanol / other products would form / the reaction does not occur under standard conditions ✓

**(c)**
- cycle or statement: $\Delta H_f^{\ominus} = 2\Delta H_c^{\ominus}(\ce{C}) + 3\Delta H_c^{\ominus}(\ce{H2}) - \Delta H_c^{\ominus}(\ce{C2H5OH})$ ✓
- $= 2(-394) + 3(-286) - (-1367)$ ✓
- $= -279\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Award [3] for correct final answer. Award [2 max] for +279.

**(d)**
- $\Delta H_{\text{vap}} = -235 - (-279) = +44\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓ ECF from (c).
- energy is required to overcome the intermolecular forces/hydrogen bonds between ethanol molecules ✓

text:
Which substances can be produced by the incomplete combustion of octane, $\ce{C8H18}$?

I. Carbon monoxide
II. Carbon (soot)
III. Water

A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: **D.** In a limited supply of oxygen the carbon is only partially oxidized, to CO or C, while the hydrogen is still oxidized to water. Options without III miss that water is always formed from the hydrogen in the fuel.

text:
The standard enthalpy change of combustion of methane is $-891\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and its molar mass is $16.05\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

What is the specific energy of methane, in $\text{kJ g}^{-1}$?

A. 0.0180
B. 55.5
C. 891
D. 14 300
ms: **B.** Specific energy is energy released per unit mass: $891 / 16.05 = 55.5\ \text{kJ g}^{-1}$. A divides the wrong way round, C is the energy per mole, and D multiplies instead of dividing.

text:
Which half-equation represents the reaction at the negative electrode (anode) of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte?

A. $\ce{H2(g) -> 2H+(aq) + 2e-}$
B. $\ce{O2(g) + 4H+(aq) + 4e- -> 2H2O(l)}$
C. $\ce{2H+(aq) + 2e- -> H2(g)}$
D. $\ce{2H2O(l) -> O2(g) + 4H+(aq) + 4e-}$
ms: **A.** Hydrogen is the fuel and is oxidized at the anode, releasing electrons into the external circuit. B is the cathode reaction (reduction of oxygen); C and D are the reverse of the fuel cell reactions (as in electrolysis of water).

text:
Which statements about biofuels are correct?

I. Ethanol for use as a biofuel can be produced by the fermentation of glucose: $\ce{C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2}$.
II. Biofuels can be considered carbon neutral if the carbon dioxide released on combustion equals that absorbed by photosynthesis as the crop grew.
III. The combustion of biofuels does not produce carbon dioxide.

A. I and II only
B. I and III only
C. II and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: **A.** Fermentation of glucose by yeast gives ethanol and carbon dioxide (I), and the carbon released when a biofuel burns was recently removed from the atmosphere by photosynthesis (II). III is false: biofuels contain carbon and their complete combustion produces $\ce{CO2}$.

The standard enthalpy changes of combustion of the first four straight-chain alcohols are plotted against the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.

**(b)**
- $-3330\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept −3300 to −3360. ECF from (a).

**(c)**
- each extra $\ce{CH2}$ requires one extra C–C and two extra C–H bonds to be broken (and extra O=O) ✓
- one extra $\ce{CO2}$ and one extra $\ce{H2O}$ are formed, and the energy released by these extra C=O and O–H bonds is greater than that absorbed, by a constant amount ✓

**(d)**

text:
Octane, $\ce{C8H18}$ ($M = 114.26\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$), is a major component of petrol (gasoline).

(a) Write an equation for the complete combustion of octane. [1]

(b) Write an equation for the incomplete combustion of octane in which carbon monoxide and water are the only products. [1]

(c) Explain why carbon monoxide is toxic. [1]

(d) Calculate the mass, in kg, of carbon dioxide produced when $1.00\ \text{kg}$ of octane undergoes complete combustion. [3]

(e) Explain how carbon dioxide in the atmosphere contributes to the greenhouse effect. [2]

- $\ce{2C8H18 + 25O2 -> 16CO2 + 18H2O}$ ✓ Accept $\ce{C8H18 + 25/2O2 -> 8CO2 + 9H2O}$.

**(b)**
- $\ce{2C8H18 + 17O2 -> 16CO + 18H2O}$ ✓ Accept $\ce{C8H18 + 17/2O2 -> 8CO + 9H2O}$.

**(c)**
- CO binds (strongly/irreversibly) to haemoglobin, reducing the transport of oxygen in the blood ✓

**(d)**

Hydrogen and methane are both gaseous fuels.

| Fuel | $\Delta H_c^{\ominus}$ / $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ | $M$ / $\text{g mol}^{-1}$ |

| $\ce{H2(g)}$ | $-286$ | 2.02 |
| $\ce{CH4(g)}$ | $-891$ | 16.05 |

(b) Calculate the energy density, in $\text{kJ dm}^{-3}$, of each fuel as a gas at 298 K and 100 kPa. The molar volume of an ideal gas under these conditions is $24.8\ \text{dm}^3\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. [2]

(c) Using your answers to (a) and (b), discuss one advantage and one disadvantage of hydrogen as a fuel for vehicles. [2]

text:
Which change has a positive entropy change, $\Delta S$?

A. $\ce{H2O(g) -> H2O(l)}$
B. $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g)}$
C. $\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$
D. $\ce{Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s)}$
ms: **C.** A gas is produced from a solid, so matter and energy become more dispersed and entropy increases. A (condensation), B (4 mol gas → 2 mol gas) and D (ions in solution forming a solid) all decrease entropy.

text:
Standard entropy values are given.

| Substance | $S^{\ominus}$ / $\text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$ |
|---|---|
| $\ce{N2(g)}$ | 191.6 |
| $\ce{H2(g)}$ | 130.7 |
| $\ce{NH3(g)}$ | 192.8 |

What is $\Delta S^{\ominus}$, in $\text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$, for the reaction $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g)}$?

A. $+198.1$
B. $-198.1$
C. $-129.5$
D. $+63.3$
ms: **B.** $\Delta S^{\ominus} = 2(192.8) - [191.6 + 3(130.7)] = 385.6 - 583.7 = -198.1\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$, consistent with fewer moles of gas. A reverses the subtraction, C ignores all coefficients, and D ignores the coefficient of $\ce{H2}$.

text:
For a reaction, both $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ are positive. Assuming they do not change with temperature, which statement is correct?

A. The reaction is spontaneous at all temperatures.
B. The reaction is spontaneous only at high temperatures.
C. The reaction is spontaneous only at low temperatures.
D. The reaction is not spontaneous at any temperature.
ms: **B.** $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$; with both positive, $\Delta G$ is negative only when $T\Delta S > \Delta H$, i.e. above $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$. A applies when $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$, C when both are negative, and D when $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S < 0$.

text:
The equilibrium constant, K, for a reaction is $1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ at 298 K.

What is the value of $\Delta G^{\ominus}$, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, for the reaction at this temperature? ($R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)

A. $-17.1$
B. $-7.43$
C. $+7.43$
D. $+17.1$
ms: **D.** $\Delta G^{\ominus} = -RT\ln K = -8.31 \times 298 \times \ln(1.0 \times 10^{-3}) = +1.71 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J mol}^{-1} = +17.1\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$; $K < 1$ means $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ is positive. B and C come from using $\log_{10}$ instead of $\ln$, and A has the wrong sign.

text:
The graph shows how the standard Gibbs energy change, $\Delta G^{\ominus}$, for the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate varies with temperature. It assumes that $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ and $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ do not change with temperature.

$$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$

![Straight line graph of ΔG against temperature from 178 kJ/mol at 0 K, crossing zero near 1110 K and reaching −46 kJ/mol at 1400 K](qbank/img/gen_chem_R1.4_5.svg)

(a) Determine the temperature above which the decomposition is spontaneous. [1]

(b) Determine the value of $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ for the reaction, giving a reason for your method. [1]

(c) Determine $\Delta S^{\ominus}$, in $\text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$, from the gradient of the line. [2]

(d) Explain, with reference to the equation, the sign of $\Delta S^{\ominus}$. [1]

(e) Calculate the equilibrium constant, K, for the reaction at 1300 K. ($R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$) [2]

(f) Suggest why the line is only an approximation at high temperatures. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- about 1110 K (where $\Delta G^{\ominus} = 0$) ✓ Accept 1090 – 1130 K.

**(b)**
- $+178\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, from the intercept at $T = 0$, because $\Delta G^{\ominus} = \Delta H^{\ominus}$ when $T = 0$ ✓ Accept 175 – 181.

**(c)**
- gradient $= -0.160\ \text{kJ K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$ (e.g. $\dfrac{-30 - 178}{1300 - 0}$) ✓
- $\Delta S^{\ominus} = -\text{gradient} = +160\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Accept 150 – 170. Positive sign and correct units/conversion required for M2.

**(d)**
- a gas is produced from a solid, so the products are more dispersed / have more possible arrangements ✓

**(e)**
- $\Delta G^{\ominus}(1300\ \text{K}) = -30\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (from graph or $178 - 1300 \times 0.160$) **and** $\ln K = \dfrac{30\,000}{8.31 \times 1300} = 2.78$ ✓
- $K = 16$ ✓

Accept 13 – 20 depending on value read from graph. ECF from (b) and (c). Award [1 max] if kJ are not converted to J ($K \approx 1.0$).

**(f)**
- $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ and $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ change with temperature (e.g. entropies of substances increase with temperature) ✓

text:
Nitrogen dioxide dimerizes to dinitrogen tetroxide:

$$\ce{2NO2(g) <=> N2O4(g)}$$

| Substance | $\Delta H_f^{\ominus}$ / $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ | $S^{\ominus}$ / $\text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\ce{NO2(g)}$ | $+33.2$ | 240.1 |
| $\ce{N2O4(g)}$ | $+9.2$ | 304.4 |

(a) Predict, with a reason, the sign of $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ for the forward reaction. [1]

(b) Calculate $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ for the forward reaction. [1]

(c) Calculate $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ for the forward reaction. [1]

(d) Calculate $\Delta G^{\ominus}$, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, at 298 K. [2]

(e) Determine the temperature above which the forward reaction is not spontaneous. [2]

(f) Calculate the equilibrium constant, K, at 298 K. ($R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$) [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- negative **and** 2 mol of gas form 1 mol of gas / fewer gas particles ✓

**(b)**
- $\Delta H^{\ominus} = 9.2 - 2(33.2) = -57.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

**(c)**
- $\Delta S^{\ominus} = 304.4 - 2(240.1) = -175.8\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$ ✓

**(d)**
- $\Delta G^{\ominus} = -57.2 - 298 \times (-0.1758)$ ✓
- $= -4.8\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Award [1 max] for an answer that does not convert $\Delta S$ from J to kJ. ECF from (b) and (c).

**(e)**
- $\Delta G^{\ominus} = 0$ when $T = \dfrac{\Delta H^{\ominus}}{\Delta S^{\ominus}} = \dfrac{-57.2}{-0.1758}$ ✓
- $T = 325\ \text{K}$ (the reaction is not spontaneous above 325 K) ✓

ECF from (b) and (c).

**(f)**
- $\ln K = -\dfrac{\Delta G^{\ominus}}{RT} = \dfrac{4810}{8.31 \times 298} = 1.94$ ✓
- $K = 7.0$ ✓

Accept 6.8 – 7.0. ECF from (d).

text:
Ice melts at 273 K: $\ce{H2O(s) -> H2O(l)}$, $\Delta H^{\ominus} = +6.01\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

(a) The standard entropy of $\ce{H2O(g)}$ is $188.8\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$ and that of $\ce{H2O(l)}$ is $70.0\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. Explain why the entropy of the gas is much greater than that of the liquid. [2]

(b) At 273 K, ice and water are in equilibrium so $\Delta G = 0$. Calculate the entropy change of melting, in $\text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. [2]

(c) Calculate $\Delta G$ for the melting of ice at 263 K, assuming $\Delta H$ and $\Delta S$ do not change with temperature, and deduce whether ice melts spontaneously at this temperature. [2]

(d) Melting is endothermic. Explain, in terms of $\Delta H$ and $T\Delta S$, why ice melts spontaneously above 273 K. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- particles in a gas are much more widely spread out / dispersed and move freely in all directions ✓
- so there are many more possible arrangements (ways of distributing energy/matter) in the gas ✓

**(b)**
- $0 = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ so $\Delta S = \dfrac{\Delta H}{T} = \dfrac{6010}{273}$ ✓
- $\Delta S = +22.0\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$ ✓

**(c)**
- $\Delta G = 6.01 - 263 \times 0.0220 = +0.22\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓
- $\Delta G$ is positive so ice does not melt spontaneously at 263 K ✓

ECF from (b). Accept +0.2 to +0.23.

**(d)**
- $\Delta S$ is positive so $T\Delta S$ increases as temperature increases ✓
- above 273 K, $T\Delta S > \Delta H$ so $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ is negative ✓

text:
For the Haber process:

$$\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)} \qquad \Delta H^{\ominus} = -92.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1},\ \Delta S^{\ominus} = -198.1\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$$

Assume $\Delta H^{\ominus}$ and $\Delta S^{\ominus}$ do not change with temperature. $R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.

(a) Calculate $\Delta G^{\ominus}$, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, at 298 K. [2]

(b) Calculate the equilibrium constant, K, at 298 K. [2]

(c) Calculate $\Delta G^{\ominus}$ and K at 700 K. [2]

(d) Industrially the process is operated at about 700 K. Explain why, despite your answer to (c). [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- $\Delta G^{\ominus} = -92.2 - 298 \times (-0.1981)$ ✓
- $= -33.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

**(b)**
- $\ln K = \dfrac{33\,200}{8.31 \times 298} = 13.4$ ✓
- $K = 6.6 \times 10^{5}$ ✓

Accept $6.5 \times 10^{5}$ to $6.7 \times 10^{5}$; accept answers in the range $6 \times 10^{5}$ to $7 \times 10^{5}$ arising from rounding of $\ln K$. ECF from (a).

**(c)**
- $\Delta G^{\ominus} = -92.2 + 700 \times 0.1981 = +46.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓
- $K = e^{-46\,500/(8.31 \times 700)} = 3.4 \times 10^{-4}$ ✓

Accept $3.3 \times 10^{-4}$ to $3.5 \times 10^{-4}$.

**(d)**
- at 298 K the rate is far too slow (too few particles have $E \ge E_a$, even with a catalyst) ✓
- 700 K is a compromise giving an acceptable rate; the low K/yield is offset by using high pressure (and recycling unreacted gases) ✓

text:
$4.0\ \text{g}$ of hydrogen gas reacts with $16.0\ \text{g}$ of oxygen gas.

$$\ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l)}$$

What is the maximum mass of water that can be formed? ($M_r$: $\ce{H2}$ = 2.02, $\ce{O2}$ = 32.00, $\ce{H2O}$ = 18.02)

A. 9.0 g
B. 18.0 g
C. 20.0 g

text:
Ethanol can be produced by fermentation:

$$\ce{C6H12O6(aq) -> 2C2H5OH(aq) + 2CO2(g)}$$

($M_r$: $\ce{C6H12O6}$ = 180.18, $\ce{C2H5OH}$ = 46.08, $\ce{CO2}$ = 44.01)

text:
A student heated a sample of hydrated magnesium sulfate, $\ce{MgSO4.xH2O}$, in a crucible to remove the water of crystallization.

| Measurement | Mass / g |
|---|---|
| Empty crucible | 22.35 |
| Crucible + hydrated salt | 24.81 |
| Crucible + residue after 1st heating | 23.71 |
| Crucible + residue after 2nd heating | 23.56 |
| Crucible + residue after 3rd heating | 23.55 |
| Crucible + residue after 4th heating | 23.55 |

(a) Explain why the crucible was heated repeatedly until there was no further change in mass. [1]

(b) Calculate the mass of water removed and the mass of anhydrous magnesium sulfate. [1]

(c) Determine the value of x. ($M_r$: $\ce{MgSO4}$ = 120.38, $\ce{H2O}$ = 18.02) [3]

(d) If heated too strongly, magnesium sulfate decomposes: $\ce{MgSO4(s) -> MgO(s) + SO3(g)}$. Predict, with a reason, the effect on the value of x obtained if some decomposition occurred. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- to ensure that all the water of crystallization has been removed / the reaction is complete ✓

**(b)**
- water: $24.81 - 23.55 = 1.26\ \text{g}$ **and** anhydrous $\ce{MgSO4}$: $23.55 - 22.35 = 1.20\ \text{g}$ ✓

**(c)**
- $n(\ce{MgSO4}) = \dfrac{1.20}{120.38} = 9.97 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $n(\ce{H2O}) = \dfrac{1.26}{18.02} = 0.0699\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- ratio $= 7.01$ so $x = 7$ ✓

ECF from (b). Integer answer required for M3.

**(d)**
- the mass of residue would be lower / the mass loss (attributed to water) would be greater ✓
- so the calculated ratio of water to $\ce{MgSO4}$ and the value of x would be too high ✓

tname: How much? The amount of chemical change
text:
Iron is extracted from iron(III) oxide in the blast furnace:

$$\ce{Fe2O3(s) + 3CO(g) -> 2Fe(l) + 3CO2(g)}$$

In a laboratory-scale model, $1.00\ \text{kg}$ of $\ce{Fe2O3}$ ($M = 159.70\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) reacted with $450\ \text{g}$ of CO ($M = 28.01\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$). $520\ \text{g}$ of iron ($M = 55.85\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) was obtained.

(a) Show that carbon monoxide is the limiting reactant. [2]

(b) Calculate the theoretical mass of iron that could be obtained. [2]

(c) Calculate the percentage yield of iron. [1]

(d) Calculate the atom economy for the production of iron. [2]

(e) Outline why a reaction can have a high percentage yield but a low atom economy. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- $n(\ce{Fe2O3}) = \dfrac{1000}{159.70} = 6.26\ \text{mol}$ **and** $n(\ce{CO}) = \dfrac{450}{28.01} = 16.1\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- $6.26\ \text{mol}$ $\ce{Fe2O3}$ needs $18.8\ \text{mol}$ CO, which is more than is available, so CO is limiting ✓

Accept equivalent reasoning, e.g. $16.1/3 = 5.36 < 6.26/1$.

**(b)**
- $n(\ce{Fe}) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 16.07 = 10.7\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- mass $= 10.71 \times 55.85 = 598\ \text{g}$ ✓

**(c)**
- $\dfrac{520}{598} \times 100 = 87.0\%$ ✓ Accept 86.9 – 87.0%. ECF from (b).

**(d)**
- $\dfrac{2 \times 55.85}{159.70 + 3 \times 28.01}$ / $\dfrac{111.70}{243.73}$ ✓
- $= 45.8\%$ ✓

**(e)**
- percentage yield compares actual with theoretical product, whereas atom economy measures the proportion of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product; a reaction can go to completion but still produce a large mass of by-product ($\ce{CO2}$ here) ✓

tname: How much? The amount of chemical change
text:
An antacid tablet of mass $1.750\ \text{g}$ contains calcium carbonate. The tablet was added to $50.00\ \text{cm}^3$ of $1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ hydrochloric acid (an excess). When the reaction was complete, the solution was made up to $250.0\ \text{cm}^3$ with distilled water. $25.00\ \text{cm}^3$ portions of this solution required a mean titre of $18.40\ \text{cm}^3$ of $0.100\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\ce{NaOH(aq)}$ for neutralization.

Assume that no other substance in the tablet reacts with the acid.

(a) Write an equation for the reaction of calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid. [1]

(b) Calculate the amount, in mol, of NaOH used in the titration. [1]

(c) Calculate the amount, in mol, of HCl remaining in the $250.0\ \text{cm}^3$ solution. [1]

(d) Calculate the amount, in mol, of HCl that reacted with the calcium carbonate. [1]

(e) Calculate the mass, in g, of calcium carbonate ($M = 100.09\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) in the tablet. [2]

(f) Calculate the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in the tablet. [1]

(g) Suggest why a back titration is used rather than titrating the tablet directly with acid. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- $\ce{CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)}$ ✓

**(b)**
- $n(\ce{NaOH}) = 0.100 \times 0.01840 = 1.84 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$ ✓

**(c)**
- $1.84 \times 10^{-3} \times 10 = 0.0184\ \text{mol}$ ✓

**(d)**
- $0.0500 - 0.0184 = 0.0316\ \text{mol}$ ✓

**(e)**
- $n(\ce{CaCO3}) = \dfrac{0.0316}{2} = 0.0158\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- mass $= 0.0158 \times 100.09 = 1.58\ \text{g}$ ✓

**(f)**
- $\dfrac{1.58}{1.750} \times 100 = 90.4\%$ ✓ Accept 90.3 – 90.4%. ECF from (e).

**(g)**
- calcium carbonate is insoluble / reacts slowly, so the end-point of a direct titration would be difficult to detect ✓

Apply ECF throughout.

tname: How much? The amount of chemical change
text:
Some car airbags inflate when sodium azide, $\ce{NaN3}$, decomposes:

$$\ce{2NaN3(s) -> 2Na(s) + 3N2(g)}$$

An airbag requires $60.0\ \text{dm}^3$ of nitrogen. Assume the molar volume of the gas under the conditions is $24.8\ \text{dm}^3\ \text{mol}^{-1}$.

(a) Calculate the amount, in mol, of nitrogen required. [1]

(b) Calculate the mass of sodium azide ($M = 65.02\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) needed. [2]

(c) The sodium formed is removed by reaction with potassium nitrate:

$$\ce{10Na(s) + 2KNO3(s) -> K2O(s) + 5Na2O(s) + N2(g)}$$

Calculate the mass of potassium nitrate ($M = 101.11\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) needed to react with all the sodium formed in (b). [2]

(d) Suggest why the sodium must be removed. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- $n(\ce{N2}) = \dfrac{60.0}{24.8} = 2.42\ \text{mol}$ ✓

**(b)**
- $n(\ce{NaN3}) = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 2.42 = 1.61\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- mass $= 1.613 \times 65.02 = 105\ \text{g}$ ✓

ECF from (a).

**(c)**
- $n(\ce{Na}) = 1.61\ \text{mol}$ so $n(\ce{KNO3}) = \dfrac{1.61}{5} = 0.323\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- mass $= 0.323 \times 101.11 = 32.6\ \text{g}$ ✓

ECF from (b).

**(d)**
- sodium is very reactive / reacts (violently) with water/moisture to form corrosive NaOH and flammable hydrogen ✓

tname: How fast? The rate of chemical change
text:
Which change increases the rate of a reaction mainly by increasing the frequency of collisions, **without** changing the proportion of collisions with energy greater than or equal to the activation energy?

A. Increasing the temperature
B. Adding a catalyst
C. Increasing the concentration of a reactant
D. Increasing the temperature and adding a catalyst
ms: **C.** A higher concentration means more particles per unit volume and so more frequent collisions, but the energy distribution is unchanged. A higher temperature (A) increases the proportion of particles with $E \ge E_a$, and a catalyst (B) lowers $E_a$, which also increases that proportion.

tname: How fast? The rate of chemical change
text:
The Maxwell–Boltzmann distributions for the same sample of gas at two different temperatures, X and Y, are shown.

![Two Maxwell–Boltzmann curves: X is tall and narrow, Y is lower and broader, with Ea marked to the right](qbank/img/gen_chem_R2.2_2.svg)

Which statement is correct?

A. Y is at the higher temperature and a greater proportion of particles have energy greater than or equal to $E_a$.
B. X is at the higher temperature because its peak is higher.
C. The total area under curve Y is greater than under curve X.
D. Y shows the same sample at the same temperature as X with a catalyst added.
ms: **A.** At higher temperature the curve flattens and its peak moves to higher energy, so the area to the right of $E_a$ increases. B confuses peak height with temperature; C is wrong because the total area represents the total number of particles, which is unchanged; D is wrong because a catalyst does not change the distribution, it lowers $E_a$.

tname: How fast? The rate of chemical change
text:
The rate equation for a reaction is $\text{rate} = k[\text{A}]^2[\text{B}]$. Concentrations are in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and time in s.

What are the units of the rate constant, k?

A. $\text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$
B. $\text{mol}^{-1}\ \text{dm}^{3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$
C. $\text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{dm}^{6}\ \text{s}^{-1}$
D. $\text{mol}^{2}\ \text{dm}^{-6}\ \text{s}^{-1}$
ms: **C.** $k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\text{A}]^2[\text{B}]} = \dfrac{\text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^3} = \text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{dm}^{6}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ for this third-order reaction. A is the unit of rate, B is for a second-order reaction, and D inverts the concentration units.

tname: How fast? The rate of chemical change
text:
The following initial rate data were obtained for the reaction $\ce{A + B -> C}$.

| Experiment | $[\text{A}]$ / $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ | $[\text{B}]$ / $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ | Initial rate / $\text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.10 | 0.10 | $2.0 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| 2 | 0.20 | 0.10 | $8.0 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| 3 | 0.20 | 0.30 | $8.0 \times 10^{-4}$ |

What is the rate equation?

A. $\text{rate} = k[\text{A}]$
B. $\text{rate} = k[\text{A}]^2$
C. $\text{rate} = k[\text{A}][\text{B}]$
D. $\text{rate} = k[\text{A}]^2[\text{B}]$
ms: **B.** Experiments 1 → 2: doubling [A] quadruples the rate, so the reaction is second order in A. Experiments 2 → 3: tripling [B] does not change the rate, so it is zero order in B. A misreads the factor of 4; C and D wrongly include B, which appears in the stoichiometric equation but not the rate equation.

tname: How fast? The rate of chemical change
text:
A proposed mechanism for the reaction $\ce{2NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ is:

Step 1: $\ce{2NO(g) <=> N2O2(g)}$ (fast, equilibrium)

Step 2: $\ce{N2O2(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ (slow)

Which rate equation, in terms of reactant concentrations only, is consistent with this mechanism?

A. $\text{rate} = k[\ce{NO}]^2$
B. $\text{rate} = k[\ce{NO}][\ce{O2}]$
C. $\text{rate} = k[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{O2}]$
D. $\text{rate} = k[\ce{O2}]$
ms: **C.** The rate is determined by the slow step, rate $\propto [\ce{N2O2}][\ce{O2}]$. The intermediate $\ce{N2O2}$ is formed from two NO molecules in the fast pre-equilibrium, so $[\ce{N2O2}] \propto [\ce{NO}]^2$, giving rate $= k[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{O2}]$. A uses only step 1 (not rate-determining); B and D ignore how the intermediate's concentration depends on NO.

tname: How fast? The rate of chemical change
text:
A graph of $\ln k$ against $\dfrac{1}{T}$ for a reaction is a straight line with a gradient of $-1.20 \times 10^{4}\ \text{K}$.

What is the activation energy of the reaction? ($R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)

A. $1.44\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
B. $99.7\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
C. $230\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
D. $9.97 \times 10^{4}\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
ms: **B.** From $\ln k = -\dfrac{E_a}{R}\cdot\dfrac{1}{T} + \ln A$, the gradient is $-E_a/R$, so $E_a = 1.20 \times 10^{4} \times 8.31 = 9.97 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J mol}^{-1} = 99.7\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. A divides by R instead of multiplying (and converts to kJ), C includes a factor of 2.303 (for a $\log_{10}$ plot), and D does not convert J to kJ.

tname: How fast? The rate of chemical change
text:
Marble chips (calcium carbonate) were added to excess hydrochloric acid at 298 K and the volume of carbon dioxide produced was measured with a gas syringe. Calcium carbonate was the limiting reactant.

![Graph of volume of CO2 against time, rising steeply from zero and levelling off at 120 cm3 after about 200 s](qbank/img/gen_chem_R2.2_7.svg)

(a) Write an equation, including state symbols, for the reaction. [1]

(b) Determine the initial rate of reaction, in $\text{cm}^3\ \text{s}^{-1}$, showing your working on the graph. [2]

(c) Explain, using collision theory, why the rate of reaction decreases with time. [2]

(d) Sketch, on the same axes, the curve you would expect if the same mass of calcium carbonate were used as a fine powder. [2]

(e) Calculate the mass of calcium carbonate used. The molar volume of an ideal gas at 298 K and 100 kPa is $24.8\ \text{dm}^3\ \text{mol}^{-1}$. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- $\ce{CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)}$ ✓ State symbols required.

**(b)**
- tangent drawn to the curve at $t = 0$ ✓
- gradient $= 3.0\ \text{cm}^3\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept 2.5 – 3.5.

**(c)**
- the concentration of acid / surface area of calcium carbonate decreases as reactants are used up ✓
- so the frequency of (successful) collisions decreases ✓

**(d)**
- curve steeper at the start (reaches its final volume sooner) ✓
- levels off at the same final volume of $120\ \text{cm}^3$ ✓

**(e)**
- $n(\ce{CO2}) = \dfrac{0.120}{24.8} = 4.84 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$ ✓
- mass of $\ce{CaCO3} = 4.84 \times 10^{-3} \times 100.09 = 0.484\ \text{g}$ ✓

Award [1 max] if the volume is not converted to $\text{dm}^3$.

tname: How fast? The rate of chemical change
text:
The rate constant, k, of a first-order reaction was measured at five temperatures.

| T / K | k / $\text{s}^{-1}$ |
|---|---|
| 290 | $6.10 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| 300 | $1.72 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| 310 | $4.54 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| 320 | $1.13 \times 10^{-2}$ |
| 330 | $2.65 \times 10^{-2}$ |

The results were plotted as $\ln k$ against $\dfrac{1}{T}$.

![Graph of ln k against 1/T: straight line of negative gradient through five points from (3.03, −3.63) to (3.45, −7.40)](qbank/img/gen_chem_R2.2_8.svg)

(a) Explain why a graph of $\ln k$ against $\dfrac{1}{T}$ gives a straight line. [1]

(b) Determine the gradient of the line, including units. [2]

(c) Calculate the activation energy, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. ($R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$) [2]

(d) Determine the value of the Arrhenius factor, A. [2]

(e) State and explain how the gradient would change if the reaction were catalysed. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- $\ln k = -\dfrac{E_a}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T}\right) + \ln A$ has the form $y = mx + c$ (with $E_a$ and A constant) ✓

**(b)**
- e.g. $\dfrac{-3.63 - (-7.40)}{(3.03 - 3.45) \times 10^{-3}}$ ✓
- gradient $= -9.0 \times 10^{3}\ \text{K}$ ✓

Accept $-8.7 \times 10^{3}$ to $-9.3 \times 10^{3}$. Units required for M2.

**(c)**
- $E_a = -\text{gradient} \times R = 9.0 \times 10^{3} \times 8.31$ ✓
- $= 75\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

Accept 72 – 77 kJ mol$^{-1}$. ECF from (b).

**(d)**
- $\ln A = \ln k + \dfrac{E_a}{RT}$, e.g. at 300 K: $\ln A = -6.365 + \dfrac{75\,000}{8.31 \times 300} = 23.7$ ✓
- $A = 2.0 \times 10^{10}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓

Accept $1 \times 10^{10}$ to $4 \times 10^{10}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ (A is very sensitive to rounding). ECF from (c). Units not required.

**(e)**
- gradient less steep / less negative because the catalyst provides a pathway of lower activation energy ✓

tname: How fast? The rate of chemical change
text:
Nitrogen monoxide reacts with hydrogen at high temperature:

$$\ce{2NO(g) + 2H2(g) -> N2(g) + 2H2O(g)}$$

| Experiment | $[\ce{NO}]$ / $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ | $[\ce{H2}]$ / $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ | Initial rate / $\text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.010 | 0.010 | $2.5 \times 10^{-5}$ |
| 2 | 0.020 | 0.010 | $1.0 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| 3 | 0.020 | 0.030 | $3.0 \times 10^{-4}$ |

(a) Deduce the order of reaction with respect to NO and with respect to $\ce{H2}$, giving reasons. [2]

(b) Write the rate equation for the reaction. [1]

(c) Calculate the value of the rate constant, k, and state its units. [2]

(d) Calculate the initial rate when $[\ce{NO}] = 0.015\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and $[\ce{H2}] = 0.025\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$. [1]

(e) A proposed mechanism is:

Step 1: $\ce{2NO + H2 -> N2O + H2O}$ (slow)

Step 2: $\ce{N2O + H2 -> N2 + H2O}$ (fast)

Explain why this mechanism is consistent with the rate equation and the overall equation. [2]

(f) State the molecularity of the rate-determining step. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- NO: second order, because doubling [NO] (expts 1 → 2, [H$_2$] constant) increases the rate by a factor of 4 ✓
- $\ce{H2}$: first order, because tripling [H$_2$] (expts 2 → 3, [NO] constant) triples the rate ✓

**(b)**
- $\text{rate} = k[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{H2}]$ ✓ ECF from (a).

**(c)**
- $k = \dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{-5}}{(0.010)^2 \times 0.010} = 25$ ✓
- $\text{mol}^{-2}\ \text{dm}^{6}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓

ECF from (b).

**(d)**
- $25 \times (0.015)^2 \times 0.025 = 1.4 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓ ECF from (c).

**(e)**
- the slow (rate-determining) step involves two NO and one $\ce{H2}$, matching the orders in the rate equation ✓
- the two steps add up to the overall equation (N$_2$O cancels) ✓

**(f)**
- termolecular / three ✓

tname: How fast? The rate of chemical change
text:
Hydrogen peroxide decomposes slowly at room temperature. The reaction is much faster when solid manganese(IV) oxide is added as a catalyst. The reaction is exothermic.

(a) Write an equation, including state symbols, for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. [1]

(b) Sketch a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve, labelling both axes. Mark the activation energies of the catalysed and uncatalysed reactions and use your sketch to explain how the catalyst increases the rate. [3]

(c) Sketch a potential energy profile showing both the catalysed and uncatalysed reactions, labelling $\Delta H$. [2]

(d) Explain why a small increase in temperature causes a large increase in the rate of reaction. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- $\ce{2H2O2(aq) -> 2H2O(l) + O2(g)}$ ✓ State symbols required.

**(b)**

![Maxwell–Boltzmann curve with Ea(catalysed) to the left of Ea(uncatalysed) and the areas beyond each shaded](qbank/img/gen_chem_R2.2_10.svg)

- curve starting at the origin, rising to a peak and approaching the energy axis without touching it **and** axes labelled number of particles and (kinetic) energy ✓
- $E_a$(catalysed) marked at lower energy than $E_a$(uncatalysed) ✓
- catalyst provides an alternative pathway of lower $E_a$, so a greater proportion of particles/collisions have $E \ge E_a$ (larger area), giving more successful collisions per unit time ✓

**(c)**

![Energy profile: products below reactants, catalysed pathway has a lower peak than uncatalysed](qbank/img/gen_chem_R2.2_10-2.svg)

- products lower than reactants with $\Delta H$ labelled (exothermic) ✓
- catalysed curve with a lower maximum than the uncatalysed curve, both starting and finishing at the same levels ✓

**(d)**
- particles have more kinetic energy so collide more frequently, but this effect is small ✓
- a much greater proportion of particles have $E \ge E_a$ (the area under the curve beyond $E_a$ increases greatly), so the frequency of successful collisions increases greatly ✓

tname: How fast? The rate of chemical change
text:
Compound A decomposes in solution at constant temperature: $\ce{A -> products}$. The graph shows how the concentration of A changes with time.

![Concentration of A against time: curve falling from 0.80 mol/dm3 at t = 0, through 0.40 at about 139 s, to about 0.07 at 500 s](qbank/img/gen_chem_R2.2_11.svg)

(a) Determine the initial rate of reaction by drawing a tangent to the curve. [2]

(b) Determine the rate of reaction when $[\text{A}] = 0.40\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$. [1]

(c) Deduce, using your answers to (a) and (b), the order of reaction with respect to A. [2]

(d) Calculate the rate constant, k, stating its units. [2]

(e) Sketch a graph of rate against [A] for this reaction. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- tangent drawn at $t = 0$ ✓
- rate $= 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓

Accept $3.5 \times 10^{-3}$ to $4.5 \times 10^{-3}$. Units required.

**(b)**
- tangent at $[\text{A}] = 0.40$ (about 140 s): rate $= 2.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ ✓ Accept $1.7 \times 10^{-3}$ to $2.3 \times 10^{-3}$.

**(c)**
- halving [A] halves the rate / rate is directly proportional to [A] ✓
- first order with respect to A ✓

Accept the alternative argument that the time for [A] to halve is constant (about 139 s from 0.80 to 0.40 and from 0.40 to 0.20). ECF from (a) and (b).

**(d)**
- $k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\text{A}]} = \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-3}}{0.80} = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ ✓
- $\text{s}^{-1}$ ✓

ECF from (a) and (c).

**(e)**
- straight line through the origin with positive gradient ✓

tname: How far? The extent of chemical change
text:
Dinitrogen tetroxide was placed in a sealed flask at constant temperature. The graph shows how the concentrations of $\ce{N2O4}$ and $\ce{NO2}$ change with time.

$$\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$$

![Concentration–time graph: [N2O4] falls and [NO2] rises; the curves cross at t2 and both become constant from t3](qbank/img/gen_chem_R2.3_1.svg)

At which time is equilibrium first established?

A. $t_1$
B. $t_2$
C. $t_3$
D. $t_4$
ms: **C.** Equilibrium is reached when the concentrations stop changing (forward and reverse rates become equal), which first happens at $t_3$. At $t_2$ the concentrations are equal but still changing (a common misconception); at $t_1$ they are still changing, and at $t_4$ the system is at equilibrium but it was established earlier.

tname: How far? The extent of chemical change
text:
What is the equilibrium constant expression for the following reaction?

$$\ce{2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g)}$$

A. $K = \dfrac{[\ce{SO3}]^2}{[\ce{SO2}]^2[\ce{O2}]}$
B. $K = \dfrac{[\ce{SO3}]}{[\ce{SO2}][\ce{O2}]}$
C. $K = \dfrac{[\ce{SO2}]^2[\ce{O2}]}{[\ce{SO3}]^2}$
D. $K = \dfrac{2[\ce{SO3}]}{2[\ce{SO2}] + [\ce{O2}]}$
ms: **A.** K is the product of the product concentrations divided by the product of the reactant concentrations, each raised to the power of its coefficient. B omits the powers, C is inverted (K for the reverse reaction), and D multiplies by coefficients and adds terms.

tname: How far? The extent of chemical change
text:
$$\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)} \qquad \Delta H = +57\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which change increases the amount of $\ce{NO2}$ present at equilibrium?

A. Increasing the pressure by decreasing the volume at constant temperature
B. Increasing the temperature at constant pressure
C. Adding a catalyst
D. Decreasing the temperature at constant volume
ms: **B.** The forward reaction is endothermic, so increasing the temperature shifts the position of equilibrium to the right (and increases K). Increasing pressure (A) favours the side with fewer gas molecules ($\ce{N2O4}$), a catalyst (C) does not change the position of equilibrium, and cooling (D) favours the exothermic reverse reaction.

tname: How far? The extent of chemical change
text:
The graph shows how the equilibrium constant, K, for a gas-phase reaction varies with temperature.

![Graph of equilibrium constant against temperature: K decreases as temperature increases](qbank/img/gen_chem_R2.3_4.svg)

Which statement is correct?

A. The forward reaction is exothermic and increasing the temperature shifts the position of equilibrium to the left.
B. The forward reaction is endothermic and increasing the temperature shifts the position of equilibrium to the left.
C. The forward reaction is exothermic and increasing the temperature decreases the rate of the forward reaction.
D. Increasing the pressure at constant temperature decreases the value of K.
ms: **A.** K decreases as temperature increases, so higher temperature favours the reverse reaction, which must be endothermic; the forward reaction is exothermic. B gets the sign of $\Delta H$ wrong; C is wrong because increasing temperature increases the rates of both forward and reverse reactions; D is wrong because K depends only on temperature.

tname: How far? The extent of chemical change
text:
For the reaction $\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$, $K = 50.0$ at a certain temperature. A mixture at this temperature contains $[\ce{H2}] = 0.10\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$, $[\ce{I2}] = 0.10\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and $[\ce{HI}] = 1.0\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$.

Which statement is correct?

A. $Q = 100$ and the net reaction proceeds to the left.
B. $Q = 100$ and the net reaction proceeds to the right.
C. $Q = 0.010$ and the net reaction proceeds to the right.
D. $Q = 0.010$ and the net reaction proceeds to the left.
ms: **A.** $Q = \dfrac{(1.0)^2}{0.10 \times 0.10} = 100$. Since $Q > K$, there are too many products relative to equilibrium, so the reverse reaction is favoured until $Q = K$. C and D invert the expression; B gets the direction wrong.

tname: How far? The extent of chemical change
text:
For a reaction at 298 K, $\Delta G^{\ominus} = -5.7\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Which statements are correct?

I. The equilibrium constant, K, is greater than 1.
II. The reaction goes to completion.
III. In a mixture in which all reactants and products are at standard concentrations, there is a net forward reaction.

A. I only
B. I and II only
C. I and III only
D. I, II and III
ms: **C.** $K = e^{-\Delta G^{\ominus}/RT} = e^{5700/(8.31 \times 298)} \approx 10 > 1$ (I). With all species at standard concentration, $Q = 1 < K$, so the forward reaction is favoured (III). II is false: $K \approx 10$ means a mixture of reactants and products at equilibrium; only very large K (very negative $\Delta G^{\ominus}$) means effectively complete reaction.

tname: How far? The extent of chemical change
text:
A student investigated the esterification equilibrium:

$$\ce{CH3COOH(l) + C2H5OH(l) <=> CH3COOC2H5(l) + H2O(l)}$$

- $0.100\ \text{mol}$ of ethanoic acid and $0.100\ \text{mol}$ of ethanol were mixed with a few drops of concentrated sulfuric acid (catalyst) in a sealed flask and left at 298 K for one week.
- The whole mixture was then titrated with $1.00\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ $\ce{NaOH(aq)}$; the titre was $35.10\ \text{cm}^3$.
- In a separate blank titration, the same volume of sulfuric acid alone required $1.60\ \text{cm}^3$ of the NaOH solution.

(a) Write the expression for the equilibrium constant, K. [1]

(b) Calculate the amount, in mol, of ethanoic acid present at equilibrium. [2]

(c) Determine the amounts, in mol, of ethanol, ethyl ethanoate and water present at equilibrium. [1]

(d) Calculate the value of K. [1]

(e) Explain why the total volume of the mixture is not needed to calculate K. [1]

(f) Predict the effect of adding more ethanol to the equilibrium mixture on the amount of ethyl ethanoate and on the value of K. [2]

(g) Suggest why the mixture was left for one week before titrating. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- $K = \dfrac{[\ce{CH3COOC2H5}][\ce{H2O}]}{[\ce{CH3COOH}][\ce{C2H5OH}]}$ ✓

**(b)**
- volume of NaOH reacting with ethanoic acid $= 35.10 - 1.60 = 33.50\ \text{cm}^3$ ✓
- $n(\ce{CH3COOH}) = 1.00 \times 0.03350 = 0.0335\ \text{mol}$ ✓

**(c)**
- ethanol $= 0.0335\ \text{mol}$; ethyl ethanoate $= 0.0665\ \text{mol}$; water $= 0.0665\ \text{mol}$ ✓

ECF from (b).

**(d)**
- $K = \dfrac{0.0665^2}{0.0335^2} = 3.94$ ✓ ECF from (c).

**(e)**
- the same number of moles appear on the top and bottom of the expression, so the volume terms cancel ✓

**(f)**
- amount of ethyl ethanoate increases (position of equilibrium shifts to the right) ✓
- K is unchanged (temperature is constant) ✓

**(g)**
- the reaction is slow, so time is needed for equilibrium to be reached ✓

Accept a reference to the catalyst only increasing the rate, not removing the need for time.

text:
The graph shows the equilibrium percentage yield of ammonia at different pressures and temperatures (illustrative data).

$$\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}$$

![Equilibrium yield of ammonia against pressure from 0 to 30 MPa for 400, 450 and 500 °C; yield rises with pressure and is lower at higher temperature](qbank/img/gen_chem_R2.3_8.svg)

(a) Describe and explain the effect of increasing pressure on the equilibrium yield of ammonia. [2]

(b) Deduce, with a reason based on the graph, the sign of $\Delta H$ for the forward reaction. [2]

(c) Determine the equilibrium yield of ammonia at 450 °C and 20 MPa. [1]

(d) An industrial plant operates at 450 °C and 20 MPa with an iron catalyst. Explain why 450 °C is used even though the equilibrium yield is higher at 400 °C. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- yield increases as pressure increases ✓
- position of equilibrium shifts to the side with fewer moles/molecules of gas (4 mol gas → 2 mol gas) ✓

**(b)**
- negative / exothermic ✓
- yield decreases as temperature increases, so the reverse (endothermic) reaction is favoured at higher temperature ✓

**(c)**
- 31% ✓ Accept 29 – 33%.

**(d)**
- at a lower temperature the rate is too slow / equilibrium is reached too slowly (even with a catalyst) ✓
- 450 °C is a compromise giving an acceptable yield at an acceptable rate (more ammonia produced per unit time) ✓

tname: How far? The extent of chemical change
text:
At 718 K, $K = 49.0$ for:

$$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$

$0.500\ \text{mol}$ of $\ce{H2}$ and $0.500\ \text{mol}$ of $\ce{I2}$ were placed in a sealed $1.00\ \text{dm}^3$ container at 718 K and allowed to reach equilibrium.

(a) Write the expression for K. [1]

(b) Calculate the equilibrium concentrations of $\ce{H2}$, $\ce{I2}$ and HI. [3]

(c) Predict, with a reason, the effect of increasing the pressure on the position of equilibrium. [1]

(d) Calculate $\Delta G^{\ominus}$, in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, for the reaction at 718 K. ($R = 8.31\ \text{J K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$) [2]

(e) $0.200\ \text{mol}$ of HI is then added to the equilibrium mixture at constant volume and temperature. Calculate the reaction quotient, Q, immediately after the addition and deduce the direction of the net reaction. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- $K = \dfrac{[\ce{HI}]^2}{[\ce{H2}][\ce{I2}]}$ ✓

**(b)**
- equilibrium: $[\ce{H2}] = [\ce{I2}] = 0.500 - x$; $[\ce{HI}] = 2x$ **and** $\dfrac{(2x)^2}{(0.500 - x)^2} = 49.0$ ✓
- $\dfrac{2x}{0.500 - x} = 7.00$ so $x = 0.389$ ✓
- $[\ce{H2}] = [\ce{I2}] = 0.111\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$; $[\ce{HI}] = 0.778\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$ ✓

Award [3] for correct final answers.

**(c)**
- no change, because there are equal numbers of moles of gas on both sides ✓

**(d)**
- $\Delta G^{\ominus} = -RT\ln K = -8.31 \times 718 \times \ln 49.0$ ✓
- $= -23.2\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ ✓

**(e)**
- $Q = \dfrac{(0.978)^2}{(0.111)^2} = 78$ ✓ Accept 77 – 78.
- $Q > K$, so the net reaction proceeds to the left (HI decomposes) until $Q = K$ ✓

ECF from (b).

tname: How far? The extent of chemical change
text:
An aqueous solution of cobalt(II) chloride contains the following equilibrium:

$$\ce{[Co(H2O)6]^{2+}(aq) + 4Cl-(aq) <=> [CoCl4]^{2-}(aq) + 6H2O(l)}$$

$\ce{[Co(H2O)6]^{2+}}$ is pink and $\ce{[CoCl4]^{2-}}$ is blue.

(a) Outline what is meant by a dynamic equilibrium. [2]

(b) Concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to a pink-purple equilibrium mixture. Predict the colour change and explain your answer. [2]

(c) When a tube of the equilibrium mixture is placed in iced water, the solution turns pink. Deduce, with a reason, the sign of $\Delta H$ for the forward reaction. [2]

(d) State the effect of adding a catalyst on the position of equilibrium and on the time taken to reach equilibrium. [2]
ms:
**(a)**
- the forward and reverse reactions continue to occur at equal rates ✓
- so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant (in a closed system) ✓

**(b)**
- turns (more) blue ✓
- $[\ce{Cl-}]$ increases so the position of equilibrium shifts to the right (to use up the added $\ce{Cl-}$) ✓

**(c)**
- positive / endothermic ✓
- decreasing temperature favours the exothermic direction; the position shifts left (to pink), so the reverse reaction is exothermic and the forward reaction endothermic ✓

**(d)**
- no effect on the position of equilibrium ✓
- equilibrium is reached in less time (forward and reverse rates increased equally) ✓

tname: How far? The extent of chemical change
text:
In the Contact process, sulfur trioxide is made by the reaction:

$$\ce{2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g)} \qquad \Delta H = -198\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

(a) Write the equilibrium constant expression, K, for this reaction. [1]

(b) At 700 K the value of K is much greater than 1. State what this indicates about the equilibrium mixture. [1]

(c) Predict and explain the effect of increasing the temperature on the value of K. [2]

(d) Explain, using Le Châtelier's principle, why increasing the pressure would increase the equilibrium yield of $\ce{SO3}$. [2]

(e) Industrially, a pressure only slightly above atmospheric is used. Suggest why. [1]

(f) State the effect of the vanadium(V) oxide catalyst on the value of K. [1]
ms:
**(a)**
- $K = \dfrac{[\ce{SO3}]^2}{[\ce{SO2}]^2[\ce{O2}]}$ ✓

**(b)**
- the position of equilibrium lies far to the right / the equilibrium mixture contains mostly $\ce{SO3}$ (products) ✓

**(c)**
- K decreases ✓
- the forward reaction is exothermic, so increasing the temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction / shifts the position of equilibrium to the left ✓

**(d)**
- increasing pressure shifts the position of equilibrium to the side with fewer moles of gas, to reduce the pressure ✓
- 3 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right, so the position shifts to the right ✓

**(e)**
- the equilibrium yield/conversion is already very high (above 95%) at low pressure, so the extra cost of high-pressure equipment and energy is not justified ✓

**(f)**
- no effect / K is unchanged ✓
